---
title: "A Positive Test Is Not a Diagnosis"
subtitle: "Why a 99% accurate test can still be wrong most of the time"
date: 2026-10-08
categories:
  - statistics
  - economics
  - health
---

Imagine receiving a text from a clinic: *Your screening test is positive.* The test is advertised as 99% accurate. It is natural to hear that number and think, “Then there is about a 99% chance that I have the disease.”

That conclusion can be dramatically wrong. When a condition is rare, a positive result from a very accurate test may still be more likely to be a false alarm than a true case. This is not a flaw in arithmetic; it is a consequence of ignoring the **base rate**: how common the condition was before anyone took the test.

This matters because screening decisions affect real people. A positive result can bring anxiety, expensive follow-up appointments, and sometimes harmful treatment. Understanding the base rate helps explain why doctors often order a second, more specific test before making a diagnosis.

## A screening program for 10,000 people

Suppose a disease affects 1 out of every 1,000 people. A hospital screens 10,000 people who do not yet have symptoms. The test catches 99% of people who truly have the disease, and it correctly clears 99% of people who do not. Those sound like excellent numbers.

Before testing, we would expect 10 people in this group to have the disease and 9,990 not to have it. The results would look like this:

| Group | Number of people | Test result |
|---|---:|---|
| Have the disease | 10 | About 10 test positive |
| Do not have the disease | 9,990 | About 100 test positive by mistake |

There are about 110 positive results in total, but only about 10 belong to people who actually have the disease. Therefore,

$$
P(\text{disease} \mid \text{positive}) \approx \frac{10}{110} \approx 9\%.
$$

In other words, after a positive result, the chance that a person truly has the disease is around 9%, not 99%.

## How can a test be 99% accurate and still mislead us?

The surprising part is that both statements can be true at once. “99% accurate” usually describes how the test behaves *within* two groups: people with the disease and people without it. But a patient wants a different question answered: “Given my positive result, which group am I likely to be in?”

The direction of the probability has changed.

The test has a 1% false-positive rate. One percent sounds tiny, but 1% of 9,990 healthy people is roughly 100 people. Since the disease is rare, those false positives outnumber the roughly 10 true positives.

This is why our intuition fails. We focus on the test result and the impressive accuracy number, while our brain quietly drops the much larger group of people who were unlikely to have the disease in the first place. Statisticians call this mistake **base-rate neglect**.

## The same test can mean different things for different people

Now imagine a doctor uses this same test for people who already have symptoms or a strong family history. Suppose 10% of this group has the disease before testing. Out of 10,000 people, 1,000 would truly have it. The test would identify about 990 of them, while producing about 90 false positives among the 9,000 people without the disease.

Now a positive result corresponds to

$$
\frac{990}{990 + 90} \approx 92\%.
$$

Nothing about the laboratory test changed. What changed was the base rate: this new group was already more likely to have the disease. A result has meaning only when combined with information about the population being tested.

## Why this is an economics problem too

Screening programs must balance benefits and costs. Testing a large low-risk population may catch some cases early, but it also creates many false alarms. Those alarms use clinical resources and impose emotional and financial costs on patients. A sensible policy asks more than whether a test is accurate. It asks who should be tested, what happens after a positive result, and whether the expected benefits justify the harms and costs.

The same logic appears outside medicine. Spam filters, fraud alerts, and airport security systems can all look highly accurate while sending many innocent cases for review when the event being detected is rare.

## The takeaway

A positive test is evidence, not a diagnosis. To interpret it, we need the test's accuracy *and* the base rate of the condition in the relevant population. When rare events are involved, even a small false-positive rate can dominate the results. That is why good decisions require asking not only “How accurate is the test?” but also “Accurate for whom, and how common was the problem before testing?”
